description.narrative: Output/s as listed by the project staff.

1.1. The government approved its first NDC committing to address climate change by (i) reducing GHG emissions by 75% by 2030, (ii) adapting to the impacts of climate change, and (iii) mainstreaming gender and social inclusion into climate action.

1.10. BSP began mainstreaming climate finance by adopting a Sustainable Central Banking Strategy and issuing regulations to incentivize green lending by banks for activities linked to the Philippines Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines, among others.

1.2. The government strengthened institutional arrangements for managing climate change by (i) enhancing links between CCC and oversight agencies (DOF and DBM), (ii) CCC reorganizing a national panel of technical experts to advise climate policy and actions and (iii) CCC upgrading the national climate monitoring, reporting, and verification system to integrate gender aspects.

1.3. The government strengthened institutional linkages with local governments for managing climate change by (i) DBM and CCC issuing guidelines for LGUs on allocating local budget for climate change expenditures, (ii) DOE and DILG requiring local governments to integrate energy efficiency and resiliency into development plans, and (iii) CCC delivering capacity development training to LGUs on GHG inventory procedures and mainstreaming climate change into planning cycles.

1.4. The government improved its public spending for climate change through (i) the General Appropriations Act 2021 and 2022 mandating the inclusion of climate change measures in all projects, (ii) DBM and CCC rolling out a quality assurance system to validate climate expenditures, and (iii) the government allocating 6.27% of the national budget to climate change activities in 2021, including for gender-responsive activities.

1.5. The government (through DOF, BSP, and CCC) strengthened its policy framework for climate finance by (i) establishing a high-level interagency task force on sustainable finance, also known as “Green Force”, (ii) DOF adopting a sustainable finance framework and issuing the country's first sovereign green bond, and (iii) BSP approving regulations for financial institutions to integrate climate change and other environmental and social risks in credit and operational risk management.

1.6. The government began implementing its NDC by adopting a comprehensive plan charting actions to reduce greenhouse gases in key sectors by 37%, a corresponding gender action plan, and a long-term national adaptation plan to scale up resilience [CCC and DENR].

1.7. To provide oversight to implement the NDC and the NAP, the government established cross-sector oversight committees, updated the national greenhouse gas inventory and reported on progress [CCC and DENR].

1.8. The government enhanced the ability of LGUs to manage climate change by expanding coverage of LGU-led LCCAPs and climate-tagged annual investment plans [CCC and DILG], increasing reporting on climate expenditures [DBM and CCC], and rolling out actionable guidance to help LGUs adopt small-scale renewables and build the capacity of LGU Energy Efficiency and Conservation Officers [DOE and other agencies].

1.9. The government increased public spending for climate change by allocating 8.8% of the national budget to address climate change in 2023 including for gender-responsive activities [DBM], establishing a unit in DOF to coordinate climate finance, including for gender-responsive climate projects, and improving the implementation of the Peoples' Survival Fund to support financing for small-scale adaptation projects [DOF].

2.1. The Department of Agriculture undertook institutional reforms to manage climate adaptation in agriculture and natural resources by (i) establishing the CRAO to oversee its climate strategies; (ii) scaling up the delivery of decentralized climate advisory and information services; (iii) integrating climate risk vulnerability assessments in provincial commodity investment plans; and (iv) mainstreaming gender across its policies, plans, programs and budgets by mandating strategic direction for gender equality and social inclusion, and a gender and development focal point system and responsibilities.

2.10. The government enhanced science-based climate diagnostics (using machine learning, AI, climate modelling, and satellite imagery) to inform decentralized planning through implementation of climate risk vulnerability assessments, for the first time, in all BARMM provinces, and risk resiliency roadmaps for 20 climate-vulnerable provinces and cities.

2.2. The DENR undertook institutional reforms to manage climate adaptation in environment and natural resources priority programs by: (i) clearly delineating organizational roles to implement its climate strategies, (ii) mandating performance indicators; (iii) rolling out a climate-responsive scorecard rating matrix based on criteria from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; and (iv) rolling out a Gender and Development Framework and Strategic Plan 2021-2025 that identifies and addresses gender gaps, and allocating 15% of DENR's annual budget for gender activities in 2021.

2.3. The government initiated reforms for agricultural insurance through: (i) the transfer of PCIC from Department of Agriculture to DOF, with a reconstituted board, to provide cost-effective services to farmers; (ii) a review of PCIC operations for 2018-2020; and (iii) the use of satellite technology to pilot post-planting validation and confirmation of damages on farms.

2.4. The government enacted the Organic Agriculture Act 2020 to modernize the regulatory and institutional framework for climate-resilient organic agriculture, including (i) a participatory certification system, (ii) an incentive scheme for producers to undertake organic agriculture, and (iii) a guaranteed annual budget allocation of ₱1.0 billion for programs.

2.5. The NCBP reduced regulatory requirements on public and private sector research and development of climate-smart technologies for non-GMO crops, with adequate monitoring and evaluation provisions.

2.6. The Department of Agriculture strengthened climate resilience across the agriculture sector by establishing a high-level climate change panel to provide strategic direction, operationalizing CRAO with an expanded mandate, permanent staff and budget, rolling out a gender responsive plan for climate action on the ground, and mandating climate information services across all regions.

2.7. The DENR improved ecosystem resilience and stability by mainstreaming the NDC and NAP 2023-2050 across DENR priority programs, activities and projects, and by promulgating 7 Republic Acts establishing new protected areas to shield biodiversity against destructive human exploitation in vulnerable ecosystems and habitats.

2.8. The PCIC doubled climate risk insurance coverage for high value crops and fisheries to almost 600,000 producers in 2022 and 2023; and launched index-based insurance modeling for better climate risk management for (a) rice production, in collaboration with PhilRice and IRRI, for climate vulnerable paddy farmers, (b) banana cultivation, for cash crop producers, and (c) fisheries, in collaboration with BFAR, for small-scale fisherfolk.

2.9. The government strengthened climate resilient agriculture production systems and technologies by structuring and staffing the NOAP and providing it with budget allocations (₱519 million in 2022, ₱900 million in 2023, and ₱922 million in 2024), rolling out a participatory guarantee system, developing a digital organic marketplace, adopting a medium-term action plan for climate-smart technologies, and approving, budgeting and initiating 39 new research projects under this plan.

3.1. The government, through DOF and DOE, initiated reforms to accelerate the transition from coal to renewables through (i) a moratorium on greenfield coal fired power plants, and (ii) the launch of the ETM Partnership to mobilize financing.

3.2. The government implemented reforms to increase investments in renewable energy through adoption of (i) DOE's strategy to increase geothermal energy, including priority status in the electricity market and an innovative finance scheme to mitigate key exploration risks for investors, and (ii) an LLDA Board resolution to open the largest lake in the country to sustainable development of FPVs.

3.3. The government implemented reforms to enable greater renewable energy entrance into the grid and electricity market by (i) the ERC implementing the Green Energy Option Program, which allows end-users to choose renewable sources of electricity, and (ii) the DOE rolling out new requirements for competitive and transparent grid services procurement to support additional variable renewable energy.

3.4. To reduce fossil fuel use in the transport sector, the government, through DOE and DOTr, implemented the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Act 2019 by establishing (i) a system for development of fuel economy standards, (ii) regulations for the standardized development and operation of electric vehicle charging stations, and (iii) a comprehensive classification and registration system for electric vehicles.

3.5. The government submitted an investment plan on energy transition to the CIF Accelerating Coal Transition Program to help phase down coal. The plan, which the CIF subsequently endorsed, aims to achieve energy security and a just transition considering gender equity.

3.6. To further promote investments in renewable energy, the government launched the Philippine Energy Plan 2023-2050, issued regulations to develop environmentally sustainable floating solar photovoltaic (FPV) in Laguna Lake and offshore wind to begin development, and conducted the Green Energy Auction Program (GEAP), including FPV.

3.7. To increase renewable energy penetration into the grid, the government developed regulatory framework to procure reserve capacity by conducting a competitive bidding and launching a reserve market.

3.8. The government implemented reforms to support universal access to clean energy by approving the National Total Electrification Roadmap 2023-2032, approving regulations for the off-grid area to rationalize subsidy including promotion of renewable energy, conducted the first competitive bidding for Micro Grid Service Providers (MGSP) in unserved and underserved off-grid areas, and issued revised rules and guidelines to set renewable energy portfolio standard in off-grid area.

3.9. The government implemented reforms to reduce energy consumption by adopting the Philippines National Energy Efficiency and Conservation Roadmap and Action Plan (2023-2050), and mandated gender responsiveness, strengthening gender equality, diversity and inclusion for government workers in the energy sector, and adopting new guidelines incentivizing electric vehicles and a gender-sensitive and inclusive design standard for electric buses as part of the Davao Public Transport Modernization Project which can be scaled across cities through DOTR

Action 1: The government approved its first NDC committing to address climate change by (i) reducing GHG emissions by 75% by 2030, (ii) adapting to the impacts of climate change, and (iii) mainstreaming gender and social inclusion into climate action.
Action 2: The government strengthened institutional arrangements for managing climate change by (i) enhancing links between CCC and oversight agencies (DOF and DBM), (ii) CCC reorganizing a national panel of technical experts to advise climate policy and actions and (iii) CCC upgrading the national climate monitoring, reporting, and verification system to integrate gender aspects.
Action 3: The government strengthened institutional linkages with local governments for managing climate change by (i) DBM and CCC issuing guidelines for LGUs on allocating local budget for climate change expenditures, (ii) DOE and DILG requiring local governments to integrate energy efficiency and resiliency into development plans, and (iii) CCC delivering capacity development training to LGUs on GHG inventory procedures and mainstreaming climate change into planning cycles.
Action 4: The government improved its public spending for climate change through (i) the General Appropriations Act 2021 and 2022 mandating the inclusion of climate change measures in all projects, (ii) DBM and CCC rolling out a quality assurance system to validate climate expenditures, and (iii) the government allocating 6.27% of the national budget to climate change activities in 2021, including for gender-responsive activities.
Action 5: The government (through DOF, BSP, and CCC) strengthened its policy framework for climate finance by (i) establishing a high-level interagency task force on sustainable finance, also known as “Green Force”, (ii) DOF adopting a sustainable finance framework and issuing the country's first sovereign green bond, and (iii) BSP approving regulations for financial institutions to integrate climate change and other environmental and social risks in credit and operational risk management.
Action 1: The government began implementing its NDC by adopting a comprehensive plan charting actions to reduce greenhouse gases in key sectors by 37%, a corresponding gender action plan, and a long-term national adaptation plan to scale up resilience [CCC and DENR].
Action 2: To provide oversight to implement the NDC and the NAP, the government established cross-sector oversight committees, updated the national greenhouse gas inventory and reported on progress [CCC and DENR].
Action 3: The government enhanced the ability of LGUs to manage climate change by expanding coverage of LGU-led LCCAPs and climate-tagged annual investment plans [CCC and DILG], increasing reporting on climate expenditures [DBM and CCC], and rolling out actionable guidance to help LGUs adopt small-scale renewables and build the capacity of LGU Energy Efficiency and Conservation Officers [DOE and other agencies].
Action 4: The government increased public spending for climate change by allocating 8.8% of the national budget to address climate change in 2023 including for gender-responsive activities [DBM], establishing a unit in DOF to coordinate climate finance, including for gender-responsive climate projects, and improving the implementation of the Peoples' Survival Fund to support financing for small-scale adaptation projects [DOF].
Action 5: BSP began mainstreaming climate finance by adopting a Sustainable Central Banking Strategy and issuing regulations to incentivize green lending by banks for activities linked to the Philippines Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines, among others.
Action 1: The government will increase commitment to climate action by approving its second NDC with updated climate targets and adopting a long-term strategy for climate change.
Action 2: The government will continue to strengthen oversight of the NDC and the NAP through regular reporting on progress [CCC and DENR], rolling out the NDC gender action plan [CCC] and improving linkages with public investment programming [NEDA].
Action 3: The government will continue to strengthen and expand institutional linkages with local governments for managing climate change by (i) increasing LCCAP coverage across all LGUs and (ii) improving the quality of LCCAPs in priority provinces [CCC].
Action 4: The government will increase relative public spending for climate change by allocating sufficient budget through the GAA for climate change measures, including gender-responsive activities [DBM], introducing financing strategies and climate finance tracking tools for the NDC and the NAP, and recapitalizing the People's Survival Fund, including for gender-responsive adaptation activities [DOF].
Action 5: The government will expand socially inclusive climate policy by adopting a framework for generation of carbon credits under the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets, including for LGUs [DENR and DOF], and roll-out a national approach for Just Transition [DENR and CCC].

Action 1: The government, through DOF and DOE, initiated reforms to accelerate the transition from coal to renewables through (i) a moratorium on greenfield coal fired power plants, and (ii) the launch of the ETM Partnership to mobilize financing.

Action 3: To increase renewable energy penetration into the grid, the government developed regulatory framework to procure reserve capacity by conducting a competitive bidding and launching a reserve market.
Action 4: The government implemented reforms to support universal access to clean energy by approving the National Total Electrification Roadmap 2023-2032, approving regulations for the off-grid area to rationalize subsidy including promotion of renewable energy, conducted the first competitive bidding for Micro Grid Service Providers (MGSP) in unserved and underserved off-grid areas, and issued revised rules and guidelines to set renewable energy portfolio standard in off-grid area.
Action 5: The government implemented reforms to reduce energy consumption by adopting the Philippines National Energy Efficiency and Conservation Roadmap and Action Plan (2023-2050), and mandated gender responsiveness, strengthening gender equality, diversity and inclusion for government workers in the energy sector, and adopting new guidelines incentivizing electric vehicles and a gender-sensitive and inclusive design standard for electric buses as part of the Davao Public Transport Modernization Project which can be scaled across cities through DOTR

Action 3: The government will expand renewable energy deployment by carrying out successive GEAPs to increase renewable energy capacity, including offshore wind, establishing a geothermal de-risking facility, enhancing the bidding design to scale up renewable energy through MGSP in unserved and underserved off-grid areas, and strengthening the credit worthiness of Electric Cooperatives in off-grid area.
Action 4: The government will increase the grid capability to accommodate renewable energy by developing supporting framework to accelerate investment in the transmission grid, finalizing a Smart and Green Grid Plan, developing policy and regulation to increase reserve capacity, and reduce reserve market price and its volatility.
Action 5: The government will accelerate reforms to reduce energy consumption by expanding guidelines for energy efficiency in buildings, introducing energy performance standards for industrial equipment, establishing a dedicated climate unit in DOTr and formulating a decarbonization roadmap for the transport sector, developing transportation infrastructure standards for climate, and rolling-out guidelines to prevent gender-based violence in low-carbon transport projects.
Action 1: The government, through DOF and DOE, initiated reforms to accelerate the transition from coal to renewables through (i) a moratorium on greenfield coal fired power plants, and (ii) the launch of the ETM Partnership to mobilize financing.
Action 2: The government implemented reforms to increase investments in renewable energy through adoption of (i) DOE's strategy to increase geothermal energy, including priority status in the electricity market and an innovative finance scheme to mitigate key exploration risks for investors, and (ii) an LLDA Board resolution to open the largest lake in the country to sustainable development of FPVs.
Action 3: The government implemented reforms to enable greater renewable energy entrance into the grid and electricity market by (i) the ERC implementing the Green Energy Option Program, which allows end-users to choose renewable sources of electricity, and (ii) the DOE rolling out new requirements for competitive and transparent grid services procurement to support additional variable renewable energy.
Action 4: To reduce fossil fuel use in the transport sector, the government, through DOE and DOTr, implemented the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Act 2019 by establishing (i) a system for development of fuel economy standards, (ii) regulations for the standardized development and operation of electric vehicle charging stations, and (iii) a comprehensive classification and registration system for electric vehicles.
Action 1: The government submitted an investment plan on energy transition to the CIF Accelerating Coal Transition Program to help phase down coal. The plan, which the CIF subsequently endorsed, aims to achieve energy security and a just transition considering gender equity.
Action 2: To further promote investments in renewable energy, the government launched the Philippine Energy Plan 2023-2050, issued regulations to develop environmentally sustainable floating solar photovoltaic (FPV) in Laguna Lake and offshore wind to begin development, and conducted the Green Energy Auction Program (GEAP), including FPV.
Action 3: To increase renewable energy penetration into the grid, the government developed regulatory framework to procure reserve capacity by conducting a competitive bidding and launching a reserve market.
Action 4: The government implemented reforms to support universal access to clean energy by approving the National Total Electrification Roadmap 2023-2032, approving regulations for the off-grid area to rationalize subsidy including promotion of renewable energy, conducted the first competitive bidding for Micro Grid Service Providers (MGSP) in unserved and underserved off-grid areas, and issued revised rules and guidelines to set renewable energy portfolio standard in off-grid area.
Action 5: The government implemented reforms to reduce energy consumption by adopting the Philippines National Energy Efficiency and Conservation Roadmap and Action Plan (2023-2050), and mandated gender responsiveness, strengthening gender equality, diversity and inclusion for government workers in the energy sector, and adopting new guidelines incentivizing electric vehicles and a gender-sensitive and inclusive design standard for electric buses as part of the Davao Public Transport Modernization Project which can be scaled across cities through DOTR
